english-001.text: "Certainly", not "No problem". "No problem" suggests the request could have been a problem. In luxury service, prefer "Certainly", "Of course" or "With pleasure". They sound confident and gracious. In the room: Guest: "Could we have some more bread?" — You: "Certainly, I'll bring it right away."

english-002.text: "My pleasure". The classic reply to "thank you" in luxury hospitality is "My pleasure" or "It's my pleasure" — warmer than "You're welcome" and far better than "No worries". Say it while making eye contact. In the room: Guest: "Thank you, that was perfect." — You: "It's my pleasure, Mrs Collins. Enjoy the rest of your evening."

english-003.text: "May I…" vs "Can I…". "Can I…?" asks about ability; "May I…?" asks for permission and sounds more formal. In fine dining, "May I…?" is the standard: "May I take your coat?", "May I suggest…?". "Could I…?" is a polite middle ground. In the room: Instead of "Can I take this?": "May I clear your plate, sir?"

english-004.text: "Would you care for…?". "Would you care for…?" is an elegant way to offer something, more refined than "Do you want…?". Similar options: "Would you like…?" and "May I offer you…?". "Do you want…?" sounds too direct in a luxury setting. In the room: "Would you care for a digestif? We have a lovely Williams pear brandy from Valais."

english-005.text: Never a flat "no". Luxury service avoids a plain "no". Use the structure: "Unfortunately…, however, what I can offer is…". The guest hears the alternative, not the refusal. In the room: "Unfortunately, the terrace is closed this evening because of the wind. However, I can offer you our best table by the window, with a view of the Matterhorn."

english-006.text: Instead of "I don't know". "I don't know" ends the conversation. "Let me find out for you" or "Allow me to check with the chef" keeps it going and shows ownership. Then always come back with the answer. In the room: Guest: "Is the butter made with raw milk?" — "That's a very good question. Allow me to check with the kitchen, I'll be right back."

english-007.text: Checking on the table. "Is everything all right?" invites a quick "fine". Better: "How is the venison?" (specific) or "Is everything to your liking?" (formal). Ask after the first two or three bites, not with a full mouth. In the room: "How are you finding the Petite Arvine with the char?" — the guest talks about the pairing, and you learn something useful.

english-008.text: Recommending without pushing. Soft openers make recommendations feel like advice, not sales: "May I suggest…", "If I may…", "A personal favourite of mine is…", "You might enjoy…". Give one clear reason why. In the room: "If I may, a personal favourite of mine is the Cornalin: it has the depth you enjoy in Syrah, but with Alpine freshness."

english-010.text: The emphatic "do". Adding "do" before a verb makes it warmer and more sincere: "I do apologise", "Please do let me know", "Do enjoy your evening". It's very common in British upscale service. In the room: "If there's anything else you need, please do let me know."

team-001.text: Psychological safety. Psychological safety is the shared belief that you can speak up, ask or admit a mistake without being punished or humiliated. Amy Edmondson (Harvard) showed that teams with more of it report more errors, because they hide fewer, not because they make more. Google's Project Aristotle found it was the strongest predictor of team effectiveness. In the room: A commis admits he sent table 12 the wrong main. Instead of snapping, you say: "Thanks for telling me straight away — let's fix it together." Next time, he will tell you before the guest notices.

team-002.text: SBI feedback: Situation, Behaviour, Impact. The SBI model (Center for Creative Leadership) keeps feedback factual instead of personal. Describe the specific Situation, the observable Behaviour (what you saw or heard, not what you assume), and its Impact. Then stop and listen. In the room: "Last night at table 7, you cleared the plates while two guests were still eating. The host looked uncomfortable and his friends felt rushed. How did you see it?"

team-003.text: Praise in public, correct in private. Public correction triggers a threat response: people focus on saving face, not on learning. Recognition in front of peers multiplies its effect and shows everyone what good looks like. The rule is old, but it still works. In the room: In the pre-shift briefing: "Yesterday Lucía remembered that Mr Keller is allergic to nuts before he even mentioned it — that's our standard." The pouring mistake you noticed? You mention it to the waiter one-to-one, by the service station.

team-004.text: Radical Candor. Kim Scott's framework crosses two axes: care personally and challenge directly. Caring without challenging is "ruinous empathy"; challenging without caring is "obnoxious aggression". Good managers do both at once. In the room: A friendly runner keeps arriving late. Saying nothing to protect the relationship is ruinous empathy. Radical candor: "I like working with you, and that's why I'm telling you: being late three times this week puts pressure on the whole team."

team-005.text: Autonomy, competence, relatedness. Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan) says lasting motivation grows when three needs are met. Autonomy: some control over how I work. Competence: feeling I am getting better. Relatedness: feeling part of the group. In the room: Let a waiter choose how to set up his station (autonomy), teach him to decant (competence), and include him in the staff meal conversation and the team's jokes (relatedness).

team-006.text: Herzberg: hygiene vs. motivators. Frederick Herzberg separated two kinds of factors. Hygiene factors (pay, schedules, staff accommodation) cause dissatisfaction when they are bad, but don't motivate when they are fine. Motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) are what drive people to give more. In the room: Fixing the broken staff coffee machine stops complaints — but it won't create passion. Giving your best waiter responsibility for the cheese trolley might.

team-007.text: The Pygmalion effect. Robert Rosenthal showed that a leader's expectations tend to become self-fulfilling. When you believe someone can grow, you give them more attention, harder tasks and better feedback — and they do grow. Low expectations work the same way in reverse (the Golem effect). In the room: Tell a quiet new commis: "I think you'd be good at the wine side — want to shadow me on the cellar check?" Your belief changes how you treat her, and how she treats the job.

team-008.text: Situational leadership. Hersey and Blanchard's model says there is no single best style: adapt to the person's competence and commitment on that specific task. The four styles are Directing, Coaching, Supporting and Delegating. The same person may need directing for wine and delegating for table setting. In the room: New waiter, first wine service: you show each step (directing). Experienced waiter feeling unsure after a complaint: you ask questions and encourage (supporting). Your senior: "Section B is yours tonight" (delegating).

team-009.text: Don't take the monkey. In a classic Harvard Business Review article (Oncken & Wass, 1974), a "monkey" is the next move on a problem. When a team member says "we have a problem" and you answer "let me think about it", the monkey jumps onto your back. Ask instead: "What do you suggest?" In the room: "Chef, we're out of the Cornalin on the list." Instead of solving it yourself: "Which two alternatives would you offer the guest, and at what price?" He comes back with an answer, not a problem.

team-010.text: Delegate the outcome, not just the task. Good delegation explains what "done well" looks like, why it matters, the deadline and the limits of authority. Then agree on a check-in point instead of hovering. Taking the task back at the first mistake teaches people that delegation is fake. In the room: "Please organise the wine pairing briefing for the Christmas menu: all 6 wines tasted by the team before Friday, 20 minutes max. You can open the bottles you need. Show me the plan on Wednesday."

team-011.text: Five ways to handle conflict. The Thomas-Kilmann model describes five modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating. None is always right — competing fits an emergency, collaborating fits important long-term issues. The trap is using the same mode for everything. In the room: Mid-service, two waiters argue over a table: you decide on the spot (competing). Next morning, you sit with both and redesign the section plan together (collaborating).

team-012.text: Fundamental attribution error. We tend to explain other people's mistakes by their character ("he's lazy") and our own by circumstances ("I was overloaded"). This bias poisons conflicts between floor and kitchen. Before judging, ask what situation might explain the behaviour. In the room: The pass is slow and a waiter mutters "the kitchen doesn't care". You check: a chef de partie went home sick. Sharing that context turns blame into teamwork.

team-013.text: Forming, storming, norming, performing. Bruce Tuckman (1965) described how teams develop: forming (polite, unsure), storming (friction over roles), norming (shared rules emerge) and performing (smooth autonomy). In 1977 he added adjourning, when the team breaks up. Storming is normal, not a sign of failure. In the room: Every December in Zermatt, the seasonal team arrives. Week two brings tensions about sections and closing duties. Expect it, set clear rules early, and the team reaches "performing" before the Christmas peak.

team-014.text: The peak-end rule. Daniel Kahneman's research shows we remember an experience mainly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, not by its average. A long dinner is judged by its peak and its farewell. The goodbye is not a formality — it is half the memory. In the room: design a peak — the sommelier opening a magnum at the table for a birthday — and protect the end: coats ready, a warm goodbye by name, perhaps a small truffle for the road.

team-015.text: The service recovery paradox. Sometimes a guest who had a problem that was solved brilliantly ends up more loyal than one who had no problem at all. Research shows this is not guaranteed, so never create problems on purpose. But it proves that a complaint is an opportunity, not only a threat. In the room: A corked bottle of Dézaley: you replace it immediately, thank the guest for noticing, and later offer a taste of a rare Amigne with dessert. He talks about it for years.

team-016.text: HEARD: a recipe for complaints. A model used at Disney: Hear (let them finish), Empathize, Apologize, Resolve, Diagnose. The last step happens afterwards: find the cause so it doesn't happen again. Most complaints escalate because staff jump to the solution before the guest feels heard. In the room: A guest says her steak is overcooked. Listen fully, "I completely understand, that's not what you ordered," apologise, offer a new one with a time estimate — then check with the kitchen what happened.

team-017.text: Emotional labour. Sociologist Arlie Hochschild (The Managed Heart, 1983) named the effort of showing emotions the job requires. "Surface acting" (faking a smile) drains people faster than "deep acting" (genuinely shifting your perspective). Leaders can protect the team by recognising this effort, not just the visible work. In the room: After a waiter handles a rude guest perfectly, say: "That was hard, and you stayed elegant. Take five minutes before your next table."

team-018.text: Empowerment, the Ritz-Carlton way. The Ritz-Carlton famously allows each employee to spend up to $2,000 per guest to solve a problem, without asking a manager. The number matters less than the message: "We trust your judgement." Their motto describes staff as "Ladies and Gentlemen serving Ladies and Gentlemen". In the room: Define your own team rule: "Any waiter can offer a dessert or a glass of wine to fix a problem, then tell me after service." Fewer delays, happier guests, more ownership.

team-019.text: The daily line-up. A short, standing briefing before every service aligns the team: VIPs, allergies, menu changes, sold-out items, one service standard to focus on. Ritz-Carlton hotels hold one every day across the world. Keep it under 10 minutes, energetic, and end with a clear focus. In the room: "Tonight: 62 covers, table 4 is a honeymoon, table 9 coeliac. The lamb is sold out — offer the venison. Focus of the day: wine refills before the glass is empty."

team-020.text: GROW: coaching with questions. John Whitmore's GROW model structures a coaching conversation: Goal (what do you want?), Reality (what's happening now?), Options (what could you do?), Will (what will you do, and when?). Asking good questions builds more independence than giving answers. In the room: A waiter wants to sell more wine. Goal: "Two more bottles per night." Reality: "I only recommend when asked." Options: describe one wine per table, offer pairings… Will: "Tonight I'll suggest a wine at every table."

team-021.text: From colleague to boss. Being promoted over former peers is one of the hardest transitions. Talk openly with each person about the change early, instead of pretending nothing happened. Stay warm, but stop joining the gossip and stop hiding friends' mistakes — fairness is now your job. In the room: In January, as Chef de Service, sit with your closest colleague: "Our friendship matters to me. At work I'll have to be fair with everyone, including you. If it ever feels strange, tell me."

team-022.text: Clear is kind. Brené Brown sums it up: "Clear is kind. Unclear is unkind." Vague expectations feel nice in the moment but lead to failure and frustration later. Say exactly what good looks like, and check it was understood. In the room: Instead of "Keep an eye on the water": "No glass below one third. If a table is on still water, refill without asking."

team-023.text: Feedforward. Marshall Goldsmith proposes focusing on the future instead of the past: ask for, and give, suggestions for next time. People can't change what happened, and future-focused ideas feel less like judgement. It works especially well with sensitive or experienced staff. In the room: Rather than reviewing what went wrong with last night's banquet, ask the team: "For the next banquet, what's one thing we should do differently?"

team-024.text: Spotting burnout. Christina Maslach describes burnout in three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism (detachment from the job and the guests), and a falling sense of effectiveness. Cynicism is often the first visible sign on the floor. It is a workload and environment problem, not a personal weakness. In the room: Your most passionate waiter starts saying "whatever, they're just tourists". Don't scold the attitude — ask how he's doing, check his days off, and lighten his section for a week.

team-025.text: Emotional contagion. Research by Elaine Hatfield and others shows that people unconsciously mimic the expressions and moods around them. A stressed manager spreads stress to the team, and the team spreads it to the guests. Your calm is a service tool. In the room: Saturday, full house, the printer jams. You walk, not run, speak slowly and smile at the team: "Handwritten tickets, everyone. We've got this." The room never notices.

team-026.text: Management by walking around. "Management by walking around" became famous at Hewlett-Packard and in Peters and Waterman's book In Search of Excellence (1982). Leaders who are visible on the floor hear problems early and model the standard. The goal is to observe and support, not to inspect. In the room: Every 15 minutes during service, do a slow lap: check the pace at each table, help clear a section that's behind, and give a quiet word of thanks.

team-027.text: Feedback across cultures. Erin Meyer (The Culture Map) shows that cultures differ in how directly they give negative feedback. Germans and Dutch tend to be more direct, while British or many Asian cultures tend to soften the message. In an international team, the same words can sound brutal to one person and vague to another. In the room: With a German colleague you can say "This is not correct, redo it". With a Thai colleague, the same message may land better as "Let's look at this together; maybe we can improve it." Check what was understood.

team-028.text: Structured interviews beat gut feeling. Large meta-analyses (Schmidt & Hunter) show that structured interviews — the same questions for every candidate, scored against clear criteria — predict job performance much better than informal chats. Unstructured interviews are vulnerable to the halo effect: one good trait colours everything. In the room: Ask every waiter candidate: "Tell me about a time a guest was angry. What did you do?" Score each answer from 1 to 5 before comparing — not just "he seemed nice".

wine-001.text: Switzerland's six wine regions. Swiss wine is officially grouped into six regions: Valais, Vaud, Geneva, the Three Lakes (Neuchâtel, Biel and Murten/Vully), German-speaking Switzerland and Ticino. Valais and Vaud together hold well over half of the vineyards. Each region speaks a different language and has its own signature grapes. In the room: A guest asks: "Is Swiss wine all the same?" You answer: "Not at all — from the Alpine Valais to Italian-speaking Ticino, it's six very different regions. May I start you with something from right here in Valais?"

wine-002.text: Valais: the largest wine canton. Valais grows about a third of all Swiss vines, on the steep, sunny slopes of the Rhône valley. It is one of the driest areas of Switzerland, and the warm foehn wind helps ripen the grapes. Its diversity of native grapes — Petite Arvine, Cornalin, Humagne, Amigne, Heida — is unique. In the room: "Our wine list focuses on Valais: the vineyards are just down the valley from Zermatt, some of them on terraces so steep they are harvested by hand."

wine-003.text: Chasselas, Fendant, Gutedel. Chasselas is Switzerland's most planted white grape and the pride of Vaud. In Valais its wine is traditionally called Fendant, and in German it is Gutedel. It is delicate, low in acidity and neutral on purpose: it shows the soil it grows in, from lime-blossom freshness to a flinty, mineral finish. In the room: A guest is confused: "Fendant and Chasselas?" — "Same grape, different name: in Valais we call it Fendant. Light, fresh, perfect with the raclette."

wine-004.text: Pinot Noir: Switzerland's most planted grape. Pinot Noir is the most planted grape variety in Switzerland, grown in every region. In German-speaking areas it is called Blauburgunder; the Bündner Herrschaft (Graubünden) is especially renowned for it. Expect red cherry and raspberry, fine tannins and fresh acidity. In the room: For a guest who loves Burgundy: "If you enjoy Burgundy, try a Pinot Noir from the Bündner Herrschaft — same grape, Alpine freshness, and very hard to find outside Switzerland."

wine-005.text: Petite Arvine: the salty star. Petite Arvine is a native Valais white and probably its most prestigious. It has lively acidity, notes of grapefruit, rhubarb and wisteria, and a typical salty finish. It is made both dry and sweet (from late-harvested or shrivelled grapes, often labelled "flétri"). In the room: "With the char from the lake, I'd suggest a dry Petite Arvine: citrusy and slightly salty, it lifts the fish beautifully."

wine-006.text: Cornalin: Valais' deep red. Cornalin (historically "Rouge du Pays") is a native Valais red, a cross of Petit Rouge and Mayolet. It is difficult to grow and needs warm sites, but gives deeply coloured wines with dark cherry, spice and firm, lively structure. It is one of the region's prized reds. In the room: "With the venison, a Cornalin: dark cherry and spice, with enough freshness to balance the sauce. It's a grape you'll almost only find here in Valais."

wine-007.text: Humagne Rouge vs Humagne Blanche. Despite the shared name, these two Valais grapes are not related. DNA analysis showed Humagne Rouge is the same variety as Cornalin from the Aosta Valley in Italy; it gives rustic reds with wild, earthy notes. Humagne Blanche is an old Valais white variety, delicate and discreet. In the room: A curious guest notices both on the list. You smile: "A Swiss trick — same first name, different families. The Rouge is wild and earthy, lovely with game."

wine-008.text: Amigne de Vétroz and its bees. Amigne is a rare Valais white grown almost entirely around the village of Vétroz. Producers there show sweetness with bees on the label: one bee is dry, two are off-dry, three are sweet. Its aromas often recall mandarin and orange peel. In the room: "For your cheese course, a three-bee Amigne: sweet notes of mandarin with the blue cheese. And yes — the bees tell you how sweet it is."

wine-009.text: Heida from Visperterminen. Heida (called Païen in French-speaking Valais) is the Savagnin Blanc grape, the same as in the Jura's vin jaune. In Visperterminen, just above Visp, it grows in some of the highest vineyards in Europe, up to around 1,150 m. The wines are full, spicy and fresh at the same time. In the room: "You came up through Visp on the train? The vineyards above it produce this Heida — from some of Europe's highest vines, just half an hour from here."

wine-010.text: Dôle: the Valais red blend. Dôle is a traditional Valais red made mainly from Pinot Noir and Gamay, with Pinot Noir dominant. It is fruity, supple and easy to pair. Its rosé version, Dôle Blanche, is a pale pink wine made from the same grapes. In the room: A family wants one bottle for the whole table — fish, veal and a vegetarian dish. "A Dôle: light enough for the fish, fruity enough for the veal."

wine-011.text: Lavaux: UNESCO terraces. The Lavaux terraces on Lake Geneva became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007. Locals speak of "three suns": the sky, its reflection on the lake and the heat stored in the stone walls. Dézaley and Calamin are its Grand Cru appellations, both famous for Chasselas. In the room: "This Dézaley Grand Cru comes from the Lavaux terraces — they say the vines get three suns: the sky, the lake and the warm stone walls."

wine-012.text: Ticino: the kingdom of Merlot. Merlot arrived in Ticino in the early 20th century, after phylloxera destroyed the old vineyards, and now dominates the region. Ticino Merlots range from light and fruity to rich, oak-aged reds. A local curiosity is Merlot bianco: Merlot pressed quickly and made as a white wine. In the room: "A white Merlot? Yes — in Ticino they press it straight away, so the juice stays pale. Would you like to taste it?"

wine-013.text: Neuchâtel: Œil-de-Perdrix and non-filtré. Œil-de-Perdrix ("partridge's eye") is a rosé made from Pinot Noir; the style originated in Neuchâtel. The region also releases an unfiltered, slightly cloudy Chasselas, the "non-filtré", every year on the third Wednesday of January. Both are signature wines of the Three Lakes region. In the room: A guest orders a rosé "but not too sweet". You suggest an Œil-de-Perdrix: "Dry, delicate, from Pinot Noir — the name means partridge's eye, for its colour."

wine-014.text: Müller-Thurgau, a Swiss invention. Müller-Thurgau was created in 1882 by Hermann Müller, a scientist from the Swiss canton of Thurgau, working in Geisenheim, Germany. It is a cross of Riesling and Madeleine Royale. In Switzerland it is often still called Riesling-Sylvaner and is the main white of German-speaking Switzerland. In the room: A German guest says Müller-Thurgau is German. You reply kindly: "Created in Germany, yes — but by a Swiss scientist from Thurgau, hence the name."

wine-015.text: Vin des Glaciers. In the Val d'Anniviers (Grimentz), families keep the "glacier wine", traditionally made from the old Rèze grape. It ages in larch casks that are never fully emptied: each year some wine is drawn and new wine is added, a system similar to a solera. The result is oxidative and nutty, reminiscent of Sherry. In the room: A Spanish guest tastes it and says it reminds him of Amontillado. "Exactly — the casks are refilled like a solera. Some barrels in Grimentz are generations old."

wine-016.text: Geneva and Gamay. Geneva is the third-largest wine canton in Switzerland, with vineyards surrounding the city. Gamay (the grape of Beaujolais) is one of its signatures, alongside Chasselas. Satigny, just outside the city, is one of the largest wine-growing communes in the country. In the room: "For a light red with the charcuterie, a Gamay from Geneva: juicy red fruit, low tannin, lovely slightly chilled."

wine-017.text: Why Swiss wine is rare abroad. Switzerland drinks almost all of its own wine: only around 1–2% is exported. Small, steep vineyards and high costs mean limited volumes. For international guests, this makes Swiss wine a genuine discovery they can't easily find at home. In the room: To an American couple hesitating over Bordeaux: "You can find Bordeaux at home. This Cornalin, you probably can't — the Swiss keep almost everything for themselves."

wine-018.text: Raclette and fondue: why Fendant works. Melted cheese is rich and coats the palate. A dry, light white like Fendant/Chasselas refreshes without competing, and its discreet fruit lets the cheese lead. It's also regional tradition: what grows together goes together. Heavy, tannic reds tend to clash with the cheese. In the room: A guest orders raclette and asks for a big Cabernet. You suggest gently: "May I propose a Fendant? It cleans the palate between bites — the classic Valais pairing."

wine-019.text: Four pairing principles. 1) Match weight: light dishes with light wines, rich with rich. 2) Acidity cuts through fat and salt. 3) Tannin loves protein and fat, but turns bitter with fish oils and spicy heat. 4) The wine should be at least as sweet as the dessert, or it tastes thin and sour. In the room: A guest wants a dry white with the chocolate dessert. "May I suggest a small glass of sweet wine instead? With chocolate, a dry wine would taste sour."

wine-020.text: Dried meat and Alpine reds. Viande séchée du Valais and Bündnerfleisch are air-dried beef specialities, both with protected geographical indication (IGP). Lean, salty and intense, they pair well with fruity reds of moderate tannin such as Pinot Noir or Dôle. Big tannins would make the lean meat feel drier. In the room: "For the Valais platter — dried meat, ham and rye bread — a glass of Pinot Noir from Salgesch: fruity and fresh, it won't fight the salt."

wine-021.text: Serving temperatures. As a guide: sparkling and sweet wines 6–10 °C, light whites 7–10 °C, fuller or oaked whites 10–13 °C, light reds around 13 °C, medium and full reds 15–18 °C. Too cold hides aromas; too warm makes alcohol stand out. "Room temperature" for reds was meant for old, cold dining rooms. In the room: Your Pinot Noir feels warm and alcoholic after sitting by the fireplace. "May I give it five minutes in the ice bucket? You'll see the fruit come back."

wine-022.text: The bottle ritual. Present the bottle to the host with the label facing them, and confirm producer, wine and vintage. Open it on the side table or in hand without turning the bottle, cut the foil below the lip and keep the cork silent. Pour a small taste for the host, then serve guests and finish with the host. In the room: "Your Cornalin, Mr Weber — 2021, from Domaine…" He nods. You open it quietly, pour a taste, and only serve the table once he says "Very good".

wine-023.text: Decant for two different reasons. Old wines are decanted to separate the sediment: stand the bottle upright beforehand, then pour slowly over a light source and stop when the sediment reaches the neck. Young, powerful wines are decanted to aerate them and soften their tannins. Very old, fragile wines may fade quickly once decanted, so serve them soon. In the room: A young Syrah from Valais: decant it at the start of the starter. A 30-year-old Bordeaux: decant gently at the last moment, with a candle under the neck.

wine-024.text: Corked wine (TCA). "Corked" wine is mostly caused by TCA (2,4,6-trichloroanisole), a compound that can come from tainted corks. It smells of damp cardboard, wet dog or a musty cellar and mutes the fruit. It has nothing to do with bits of cork floating in the glass, which are harmless. In the room: Before serving the host, you nose the wine discreetly: wet cardboard. "I'm sorry, this bottle is not in perfect condition. Let me bring you another one."

wine-025.text: Opening sparkling wine: a sigh, not a pop. Keep your thumb on the cork from the moment the wire cage is loosened. Hold the bottle at about 45°, pointing away from guests, and turn the bottle, not the cork. Let the pressure out slowly so it opens with a soft sigh — a loud pop wastes wine and is considered inelegant. In the room: At a birthday table you open the Champagne with a whisper-quiet sigh, then pour in two movements so the foam doesn't overflow.

wine-026.text: Describing structure. Structure is the backbone of a wine. Acidity makes your mouth water; tannin dries your gums; body is the sense of weight (like skimmed vs whole milk); the finish is how long the flavour lasts after swallowing. Guests rarely understand jargon, so translate it into feelings. In the room: Instead of "high acidity, medium body": "It's fresh and mouth-watering, not heavy — like biting into a green apple."

wine-027.text: Cellar words in four languages. Grape variety: cépage (FR), Rebsorte (DE), vitigno (IT). Vintage: millésime, Jahrgang, annata. Estate: domaine, Weingut, tenuta. Dry: sec, trocken, secco. In multilingual Switzerland you'll meet all of them on labels. In the room: A German guest asks: "Welcher Jahrgang ist das?" You answer: "Zweitausendeinundzwanzig — 2021."

wine-028.text: Malolactic fermentation. After the alcoholic fermentation, bacteria can convert sharp malic acid (as in green apples) into softer lactic acid (as in milk). This makes a wine rounder and can add buttery notes. Most reds go through it; for whites it is a style choice — many Swiss Chasselas do it, while Petite Arvine often keeps its crispness. In the room: A guest finds the Chasselas "softer than expected". "That's partly the malolactic fermentation: it turns the sharp apple-like acid into a rounder one."
